paragraphs: Swamiji warned that thousands of societies, political meetings and institutions would achieve nothing without real sympathy, a heart that feels for everyone, the heart of the Buddha and the practical wisdom of Krishna. Indians were busy copying European organisations, he said, so let him share something he had personally seen.

A group of Burmese people had been taken to London by some men who turned out to be Eurasians. These men put them on display, pocketed all the money, took them across to the Continent and abandoned them there. The Burmese spoke no European language. The English Consul in Austria sent them back to London, where they were stranded, helpless and knowing no one.

Then an English lady heard about them. She brought these strangers into her own home, gave them her clothes, her bed and whatever they needed, and then told the newspapers. The very next day, it was as if the whole country had woken up. Donations poured in, and the Burmese were helped and sent home.

Swamiji said that this kind of sympathy is the rock on which England's institutions stood: a deep love for their own people, for truth, for justice and for charity towards the stranger at the door. He gratefully recalled how warmly he himself had been welcomed everywhere in the West.

At home, by contrast, he saw little heart to build on. Start a small joint venture, and the partners try to cheat each other until it collapses. People talk of building a nation as great as England, he said, but without that foundation of love they are building on sand, and the building soon comes crashing down.
learn: Structures, startups and clubs only last if they stand on trust and genuine care. One person's kindness, like that English lady's, can move a whole society. Be the one who opens the door first.
